children.text: History

The Kundalini is depicted in ancient Indian scriptures as a coiled energy residing into the sacrum bone, and it can be thought of as each individual’s spiritual Mother. It is represented in the bible as tongues of fire above the heads of people filled with the Holy Spirit. In the Tao philosophy it is described as the Chi energy. Everyone is born with a Kundalini and with the potential to awaken it. By nourishing our connection with this energy we can spontaneously reach the state of meditation. It responds to your desire as a spiritual being to evolve and become a greater personality.
Reflection of All Pervading Power

The Kundalini is a reflection within you of the all pervading power, which is described as the power of God in many of the religions of the world, or as the flow of the energy of life in other practices.
You can feel it within

You can begin to tangibly feel the Kundalini working on your inner subtle system through sensations of a cool or warm breeze above your head and on your hands. The longer you practice expressing your desire to evolve through meditation, the more tangibly this connection can be felt in your body.

As the Kundalini rises from the base of your spine up to the top of your head, it nourishes the energy centres within you which are located on various nerve plexuses. These are the anchors of your physical, mental and emotional self, so you may feel different sensations as you meditate. You can refer to our chakra guide to help you to understand what might be happening.

children.text: The true meaning of 'meditation'

The term 'meditation' is often misunderstood, and simply associated with techniques which help us to feel more calm or contemplative. In modern times the term has become so diluted that almost anything can be coined as 'meditation'. In fact, meditation is an ancient practice which was established thousands of years ago, with the goal of  reaching a state beyond the mind, where you are in union with your spirit and the all pervading energy of the universe.

It is a state which goes far beyond simply feeling calm. It can be sublime, deeply nourishing, transformative and joy giving.This state can only be reached when the mind is completely silent, but one is totally conscious and aware. I.e. when one is in 'thoughtless awareness'.

children.text: Silence occurs in the present

Our thoughts come in waves, as a reaction to what has occurred or something that has not happened yet. In other words, when we are either reflecting on the past or anticipating the future.When we are thinking a lot, the gaps between each thought wave are very small. Before one thought has even finished, another one has started. The state of meditation occurs in the gaps between our thoughts, when the mind is in a temporary state of silence.

When the Kundalini energy rises within us, she nourishes our centres and removes any tensions within which may be causing us to think either about the future or the past. Thus, our mind starts to calm down, our thoughts occur less frequently and the gaps between them get longer.
Sahaja Yoga

The state of thoughtless awareness is a defining feature of Sahaja Yoga meditation. In Sanskrit, Sahaja means ‘born with’ ('Saha' is with, 'ja' is born), and Yoga means union. The name, therefore, translates to ‘the union which one is born with.’ This union is between your true self and the all-pervading power that permeates all elements of life. It occurs when the Kundalini passes through the final energy centre at the top of the head, and we experience the incredible state of thoughtless awareness.

While there are things we can do to facilitate this process, using our attention and desire, it is a natural and spontaneous happening. We cannot force it, but only sincerely ask for our Kundalini to rise and grant us a true state of meditation.

children.text: Energy Channels

Throughout your whole body there is a network of nerves which control all of your mental, emotional, physical and spiritual activity. It can be divided into the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems. These systems correspond to the three channels of the subtle body.The left and right channels form the sympathetic nervous system, responsible for ‘fight or flight’ responses in case of potential danger, throughout the day. The central channel is the parasympathetic nervous system, which governs our ‘rest and digest’ responses, usually activated when we sleep.

The aim of meditation is to reduce activity in the sympathetic nervous system, i.e. remove stress and imbalances, and to activate the parasympathetic nervous system, bringing complete rest to the mind and body. A truly meditative state, where the mind is completely silent, has been scientifically proven to activate this system more than an average night's sleep.
Energy centres

Another part of the central nervous system which directly relates to the subtle being, is the nerve plexuses i.e. where the nerves intersect. These nerve plexuses are what we are referring to when we say 'energy centres'. They govern specific functions of our brain and body, and it is for this reason that energy centres - ‘Chakras’- are associated with certain qualities, determined by the nerves which meet there.For example, the nerve centre which is located on the spine at the level of the heart governs our sense of love and security. These are therefore the qualities associated with the Heart Chakra.
Balancing our subtle system

By guiding the living energy within us to the centers where we are experiencing a problem, we can naturally and effortlessly address imbalances of the most subtle nature.This balancing effect takes place when we connect to the dormant energy that lies at the base of our spine, called in Sanskrit as ‘Kundalini’. The Kundalini nourishes and cleanses our system when it is awakened. This energy has been mentioned in all ancient cultures and religions, and its existence can be experienced through meditation.

children.text: Why do we feel vibrations?

When our Kundalini rises in the process of Self-Realisation she passes through our seven energy centres / chakras. The name chakra in Sanskrit means ‘wheel’. Just like a wheel, our chakras in a balanced state spin in a clockwise direction. When we encounter an obstacle, or a chakra goes out of balance this rotation is interrupted causing a blockage.

When we meditate, and use simple Sahaja yoga techniques, the Kundalini energy rises and gently brings the chakra back into balance, removing any blockages which are causing friction. This process can be felt as vibrations on our body, palms, fingers or head as warmth, tingling or pressure. Once the balance is restored that sensation can turn into a cool breeze.
Vibrations are all around us

Vibrations are not just in human beings. They are all around us. One can often feel them on a subtle level without being aware of it. You might get a positive or negative feeling from a certain place or person. These subtle feelings are vibrations. Music, nature, art, everything emits vibrations which we can feel, and which can help bring us into a balanced state.

Any Sahaja Yoga techniques you use create vibrations and work on you in a subtle way even if you can’t feel it at first. children.text: Cleansing your chakras through your feet

Just like your hands, the nerves in your feet are all connected to the chakras (nerve plexuses) on your central nervous system. Therefore by cleansing your feet, using the elements, you are actually cleansing your chakras. Each part of your foot corresponds to a different chakra, as seen in the diagram below. Using the elements

Your body is made up of the five elements; earth, fire, water, air and ether. Imbalances in our subtle system, reflected on the physical, mental and emotional levels, can be cured through cleansing techniques using these same elements. This can both reduce the time it takes us to reach the state of meditation and deepen our meditation experience.

Personalising your footsoak

You can adjust your footsoak to meet the specific needs of your subtle system by changing the temperature of the water. children.text: Early Life and family

Descended from the royal Shalivahana dynasty, Shri Mataji’s family stand out for their uncompromising adherence to the highest moral and ethical standards. Going against tradition and widely-accepted beliefs, Shri Mataji’s forefathers converted to Christianity when they saw how cruelly Hindu widows were treated at the time, especially child widows. Her father was a lawyer and scientist, fluent in 14 languages ​​and famous for translating the Qur'an into Marathi, and her mother was the first woman in India to receive an honours degree in mathematics. Both of her parents also actively participated in the struggle for India's independence from British occupation and were both jailed several times for their involvement.

In 1942, Shri Mataji, as a teenager, was detained and tortured by British soldiers for participating in the liberation movement. This was, however, considered a necessary sacrifice - so strong was the conviction that the internal liberation of people could come only after the country's liberation from foreign rule.

Shri Mataji’s husband Sir C.P. Srivastava also led an exemplary life of dedication to the highest standard of public service, serving as Joint Secretary to the Indian Prime Minister Lal Bahadur Shastri, and later as Secretary-General of the International Maritime Organization (IMO).
Shri Mataji has two daughters, whom she raised lovingly and diligently until they started their own families, before she undertook her work with Sahaja Yoga.
Sahaja Yoga

Shri Mataji was born with the complete awareness of self-realisation and right from an early age she wanted to share this precious gift with everyone. She studied human beings over a period spanning forty-seven years, as she lived and interacted amongst them, including studying medicine at university. Only after she was fully conversant with all the permutations and combinations of the human psyche did she make the final decision to trigger the opening of the Sahasrara Chakra (the seventh spiritual centre on the top of the head) within her own being that would allow her to propagate en masse self-realisation and the practice of Sahaja Yoga meditation.

fields.text: The meaning of ‘Sahaja Yoga’ can be better understood if we split it into its component parts: ‘Saha’ means ‘with’ and ‘ja’ mean ‘born’, and ‘yoga’ is the ‘union’ or ‘the technique’. So ‘Sahaja Yoga means that the technique of evolving is inborn in each of us.

children.text: Shri Mataji Nirmala Devi revolutionised the practice of yoga through the actualisation of self-realisation on the central nervous system. In the history of spirituality Shri Mataji is the first and only person to offer the experience of self-realisation en masse. She declared that it is the birth right of all human beings – regardless of religion, race, nationality or circumstance – to receive their self-realisation. She also insisted that one cannot pay for the truth or for self-knowledge, thus self-realisation has always been, and continues to be, offered free of charge.
Societal Transformation

In addition to her spiritual work, Shri Mataji gave a lot of attention to other important areas in public health and culture. She maintained that an inner state enlightened by the practice of meditation must find an outward manifestation in all spheres of human life. She created charitable organisations such as the Vishwa Nirmala Prem Ashram for destitute women and orphan children, founded international schools promoting enlightened education, established holistic health centres, created an international academy promoting classical music and fine arts, and much more. All of these endeavours complemented her global work of spiritual transformation.
Public Life and Awards

Throughout the 40 years Shri Mataji spent spreading Sahaja Yoga she received many awards and accolades from prestigious institutions and state leaders around the world. In 1996, she was nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize, and in 1997 she received personal recognition from Claes Nobel, the grand-nephew of Alfred Nobel.

How can we get closer to our Spirit and develop a quality of pure understanding and knowing oneself? Only in the state of meditation can we go beyond our mind and identifications to see oneself and touch the pure Spirit. This is called introspection. By introspection, you can remove obstacles that are within you. Like when a river is flowing, the flow is not smooth if there are stones. Difference between the soul and the spirit

The soul and the spirit are inextricably interlinked. Our body is made up of the five elements. These five elements give you your own identity, your own character, your own particularities. The sublest purest part of our being is the spirit. The causal of the five elements and the Spirit put together make the soul. Without the soul the spirit could not reflect and manifest, without the spirit the soul would be lifeless. The soul is the aspect that changes and is transient, while the spirit is changeless and eternal.
Change of perspective

It is only human that in our lives we find our identity in our appearance, our family, our religion, our job, our character… These identifications influence and shape our desires, thoughts and actions. But in reality all of these identifications come from our ego and superego. When we reach the state of meditation our mind is silent and we go beyond our thoughts, beyond our ego and superego. In this state our Kundalini power allows us to connect to the pure being within us, which is our Spirit. Our Spirit which is not this body, this mind, these identifications.

panels.title: When to do it?

children.text: How can such a simple technique be so effective?

Just like when we meditate, it is our attention and the flow of energy within us which carries tremendous power. Once we have our self-realisation and get connected to the all pervading power around us, our attention and actions take on a new power. Combined with our desire to protect our chakras and stay close to our spirit, which our Kundalini responds to, this simple technique creates a force which protects against negative energies around us.
Why before and after meditation?

In meditation we are opening up our chakras to work on them and clear them out. It is important to protect ourselves during this process. After the meditation has finished, we aim to maintain our state and so we place further protection around our chakras. This helps us not to lose our vibratory state so easily as we are less susceptible to negativity.
At what other times is it useful?

There are other moments throughout the day when it may be beneficial for us to once again raise our kundalini and put a bandhan around ourselves. When we leave our house we are exposing ourselves to a bombardment of different energies, so it is good practice to do this before we leave home. If we are going somewhere that we know to be ‘heavy’ vibrationally i.e. somewhere people experience a lot of pain/suffering like a hospital or a funeral, then it is always a good idea to do kundalini/bandhan technique first.

When we go to sleep at night our left energy channel is more vulnerable because we go into the subconscious, hence why we dream. Therefore it can also be good to do kundalini/bandhan before sleeping, especially if we are prone to bad dreams.

panels.title: Your attention is a precious resource
panels.text: It is often pulled in many different directions, leaving us feeling tired, confused and overwhelmed.\\n\\nOn an energetic level we absorb a lot from whatever we put our attention on.\\n\\nTherefore, a more still attention helps us to preserve a peaceful state within.

panels.title: Enlightened attention
panels.text: Each individual’s attention moves towards different things, generally guided by their ego, expectations and past experiences.\\n\\nWhen we bring our attention inward to our spirit, it becomes enlightened, and naturally gravitates towards things which are nourishing for us.

panels.title: Attention as a tool for meditation

children.text: Your attention is a mirror

If a mirror is whole it reflects exactly what is shown to it. In it you can see the reality of any situation, and can judge accurately what is happening. Modern life shatters the attention into different fragments, each reflecting a small part of the reality that they see. Therefore it is very difficult to reach any complete conclusions about anything. Through the healing of your attention with meditation you can begin to see your circumstances through the reflection of the whole picture. In Sahaja Yoga this is called introspection, and it is a route towards more complete self understanding and self correction.

fields.text: Modern life shatters the attention into different fragments, each reflecting a small part of the reality that they see.

children.text: Identifications can constrict your attention

Each person has a tendency to direct their attention to different things, depending on their personality, their circumstances and what they identify with. Some people respond to certain situations with anger, some with compassion, some with pity. Likewise some peoples’ attention may more quickly be stimulated by money, or intellectual arguments, or art or any number of different things. These tendencies can restrict the development of a personality and create limitations. In Sahaja Yoga, when you put your attention inside, on your spirit, it becomes enlightened. Instead of being motivated and moved by your ego, it is motivated and moved by your spirit, and has a natural tendency to drift towards things which will be nourishing for you.
The Kundalini responds to your attention

When you put your attention on a certain chakra, or internal issue whilst in meditation, your Kundalini works to nourish the chakra or fix the problem. Putting your attention on something is different from thinking about it; you must have it in your awareness but not be engaged with it. An easy way to do this is by putting your hand on the part of your body corresponding to a certain chakra. You are aware your hand is there, and it provides an anchor for your attention, but there is no need to think about it!

fields.text: Then you will realise that every day your attention is getting purified, getting powerful, getting compassionate. Normally, whatever reaction you have in your attention just disappears, and you start witnessing the whole thing, and your power of attention, through that witnessing force, acts and it works. It works not only on you, but on everything that surrounds you.

children.text: An enlightened attention is dynamic, it acts

Once your attention is enlightened by the spirit, it holds power as it is a detached, witnessing attention. Such a powerful attention can work not only inner problems but issues we see in the world around us. Like in meditation, when we put our attention on a blockage and the Kundalini cleanses it, when we put an enlightened attention on an external problem, the all-pervading energy surrounding us works on it. A fragmented attention lacks power, but a pure attention can do wonders!

children.text: You are the Divine Flute

Like the seven holes of the flute, we have seven chakras within us. For music to sound the flute has to be perfectly crafted and free of any obstruction, then the breath of the artist can produce a pure sound that touches the heart of the listener. So too, we are made like a flute and have to keep ourselves clear so that the Divine Breath can flow through us and resonate a beautiful sound that touches the hearts of others.

Like a flute, we too are perfectly crafted to sound the Divine Melody. However, we may not be aware of this essential aspect to our being. A lack of self-respect, misidentifications, or emotional indulgences may obstruct our subtle instrument. In meditation, the kundalini clears the path of all falsehood so we may resonate with the Divine Melody once again. All we have to desire is for kundalini to cleanse and nurture us, to help us surrender our ego and attachments so we may be clear and truly free.
What do we admire in music?

What do we admire in music? It is the apparent effortlessness of the musician’s work, their creative output, when they seem to be at one with the music. In this way, music is like meditation. As the musician seeks to be fully present in the (re)creation of their art, the yogi seeks to be in the state of meditation, that is, in the present moment. For the musician, in the highest act of performing there can be no burden of thought because thoughts inhibit the creative process. Whatever thoughtful deliberation was required was done in rehearsal. Even then, the act of mastering performance skills is more about becoming aware of, and peeling away the layers of thought to find the music within. This occurs spontaneously, but requires practice to develop the skill. When the musician is one with the music, the sense of ‘doing’ is lost and performing feels effortless. The help of a teacher can be useful in illuminating the way.

fields.text: As the musician seeks to be fully present in the (re)creation of their art, the yogi seeks to be in the state of meditation, that is, in the present moment.

children.text: For the yogi, thoughts are the enemy of the soul. Thoughts take us away from experiencing our self in the present moment. By peeling away the layers of thought we get to experience who we truly are, that is, the pure spirit. With the benefit of kundalini awakening, we are able to surrender our thoughts, be one in the present and truly experience our self. When our kundalini and spirit merge with the All-pervading Power, the myth of ‘doing’ is lost and we are one with the Divine. The help of a teacher can be useful, but at a minimum they must share the experience of kundalini awakening, as Shri Mataji does. Unfortunately there are many false teachers and teachings to entrap the unwary seeker.
Music and meditation exercises

If you have experienced kundalini awakening, try meditating whilst listening to music. Listen with your attention settled on top of your head. Let go of any thoughts and sustain the state of thoughtless awareness. There should be no reaction or reflection to the music. You are in meditation, in joy and one with the sound. You may feel a cool flow of vibrations on your hands and coming out of the top of your head.

children.text: A new perspective

We really understand the power of meditation when it stops simply becoming a tool for handling everyday life, but becomes a new way of experiencing your journey in this world. Once it becomes integrated into your daily life it helps you to understand yourself in a new way. This is when it gets exciting! What might happen we can’t tell you, it can only be experienced as you see yourself unfold and experience parts of yourself which you thought had gone or you didn't even know you could develop. With time, you begin to change your outlook on how you see the world and how you see yourself existing with others.
Inner Silence is enhanced

As you grow in your technical mastery of the subtle system and meditation, you begin to elongate the moment of silence between your thoughts. It's in those moments when we come into contact with the spirit and the all pervading power around us. Those brief moments of certainty become so precious, the most valuable gift you can give to yourself. If meditation remains something you only do once in a while, it’s unlikely that the experience of inner silence will increase. Nobody can do this journey for you, you can share it with others but it's unique to you and it won’t be the same for anyone else.
(Re)establish a childlike wonder at life

Ironically, as meditation becomes a daily practice, a discipline, the creativity of those experiences can expand. It becomes more unexpected each time, and thus stops becoming a ritual. Cleansing yourself on a regular basis allows for deeper and more enlightening experiences to take place, moving away from being a needs based practice. A childlike awe in life can be restored, preventing you from feeling weighed down by your existence in this world. Despite getting older, each day you can get lighter and find more wonder still.
Growth is easier and faster

When it comes to your personal growth, it is much better to meditate for five minutes everyday than for one hour once per week. Integrating meditation into your daily life means putting your attention on your spirit and connecting to the all pervading energy on a daily basis. If you are only doing this once per week, the process of personal growth is likely to be much slower and more difficult. Daily meditation is a great way to prevent yourself from getting rigid and stuck in life. With small increments in personal growth, you can replace the feeling of stagnation with constant renewal.

children.text: Although important regardless of if you are a beginner or a long-term practitioner, discipline in your mediation practice is essential if you want to experience growth and consolidation in Sahaja Yoga.
The importance of Self mastery for meditation

The qualities of self-mastery and discipline are manifest through our void chakra. In practical terms this means meditating daily, developing your sensitivity to vibrations and clearing your chakras diligently. Without this discipline your progress will be limited, and the great ocean of depth will not be touched. True transformation will only occur when you have established your foundations.
Self mastery to strengthen your spiritual foundations

Shri Mataji describes the process of self-realisation as building the roof of the house before the foundations have been prepared. You have experienced thoughtless awareness, and the kundalini has risen through your central channel and pierced your Sahastrara. However, because the foundations of the house are not yet solid, the Kundalini falls back down. In ages past, the spiritual acolyte would spend years in penance and spiritual practice under the strict guidance of a true Guru, all in an effort to purify his subtle system and clean his chakras. Only once these foundations were laid would they have any chance of the Kundalini rising.

In Sahaja Yoga, Shri Mataji created a method of en masse realisation; we can experience thoughtless awareness but often our spiritual maturity is lacking. Therefore, it is imperative that we develop the spiritual foundations of the house to support the roof. This will enable us to sustain deeper meditations and enable profound and long-lasting transformation.
Archetypes of Self-Mastery

The archetypes and role models for self-mastery are the ten primordial gurus or masters. These are great souls born on this earth at various times and in different cultures who instructed mankind on correct moral conduct. Their teachings had a profound and lasting impact on the culture of humanity and helped progress us collectively in our spiritual ascent.

Raja Janaka, Abraham, Moses, Zarathustra (Zoroaster), Confucius, Lao-Tse, Socrates, Prophet Mohammed, Guru Nanak, and Shri Sai Baba of Shirdi—they all played a significant role in the development and propagation of moral and ethical teachings in their respective cultural and religious contexts. While some details of their teachings and moral codes may vary, they all share overarching themes of moral conduct, righteousness, and ethical principles.

In the Vedic tradition these moral boundaries are referred to as ‘Maryadas’. This refers to the concept of moral and ethical boundaries, codes, or principles that guide one's conduct and behaviour. It represents the prescribed limits or standards that individuals should adhere to in order to lead a righteous and balanced life. In one example Shri Mataji described the Maryadas as a walled city; you have complete freedom within the city, but if you in your freedom venture outside it, then you cede your protection. It is to be seen in our own life how straying outside of moral conduct gets us in trouble.
Self mastery and discretion

Self-mastery as a first principle gives us the discretion and discrimination to know what is deleterious to our spiritual growth and the discipline to avoid our sinfulness. However, with regular meditation and purification of our subtle system we will no longer have the need to resist that which is detrimental to our spiritual growth because the desire for sinfulness itself will be removed. It is in this way that our bad habits just drop off; sin is no longer resisted because the seed of impure desire is removed. This is the state we should aim for as this is the meaning of becoming your own Guru.

History

All significant spiritual practices in the history of mankind have attempted to help humans achieve inner peace in their lifetime. Many spiritual practises refer to inner peace as the experience of knowing oneself. While the approaches and practices may vary, the common thread among many religions is the idea that inner peace can be attained by seeking a deeper spiritual connection, understanding one's place in the cosmos, and finding contentment within oneself and the world around them.
Why Inner peace?

What is it that makes you feel discontent? Modern society promotes consumerism and materialism rather than contentment and peace. Our satisfaction never lasts long. We hanker after the next thing constantly. We need to find a way to reset the way we feel within ourselves and remove ourselves from these pressures.

Establishing inner peace within us creates ripple effects on those around us. The well known platitude “without inner peace, there can be no outer peace” needs to be realised. Without inner peace we are susceptible to any change in our surroundings which leaves us vulnerable to feeling insecure, out of our depth or reactive.   When we are peaceful within, we are in full control of our emotions and our attention. Inner peace is our axis that keeps us steady through the ebbs and flows of life.
Daily tips to maintain inner peace
Meditate - even 5 minutes of sincere meditation can change your day
Reconnect with nature - go for a quick walk and pay attention to the nature around you
Take a deep breath - use your breathing to settle your attention
Train your attention - when you notice yourself reacting, take a step back and witness the reaction rather than engaging emotionally
Introspect - find some time in your day to notice the state of your attention and how your meditation practise is changing your behaviour and thought patterns

children.text: Pure Desire helps you to evolve

Pure desire is a power within you which motivates you to seek out and do things that will bring you the state of yoga, a complete feeling of oneness with everything around. Once your Kundalini [which is a manifestation of this pure desire] becomes awakened you can begin to feel some part of this state in your meditation.

The Kundalini works on your subtle system to clear out the blockages in your chakras which cloud over this desire and keep you away from this unified state. As it works, you can become a more and more evolved personality. Angularities in your thoughts and behaviour begin to soften and dissolve away over time.
Pure Desire brings satisfaction

Desires in general cannot be fully satiated. Every person has the need for food, shelter, company and transportation, but once these are satisfied they lead to additional needs. A person can be happy with a new car, but the enjoyment is not complete and fades over time until they find a new object or experience to desire.
Pure Desire brings you to a state that gives complete wellbeing and satisfaction from within, which is not dependent on anything to do with your external circumstances.
Evolution is not artificiality

Some people think of an evolved individual as being well read, or healthy, or hard working or one who discusses spirituality. In Sahaja Yoga a person is evolved if they have genuine depth within their personality.

This depth is usually visible through an individual’s humility, compassion, patience and the way it feels to be around them. They are nourishing to be around, and understand how to help you to overcome your problems and come closer to your own spirit.
Pure Desire brings you on a journey

Meditating for the first time to awaken your Kundalini can bring an initial powerful experience, though equally some people may feel very little to begin with. However to truly establish this state of yoga requires the development and balancing of your chakras.

This work and balancing is a journey you undertake with your Kundalini, through regular meditation, to unwind the attachments that keep you from evolving towards a higher personality. This does not mean living like an ascetic and giving up all material possessions. This is merely another form of artificial outside work. Rather, it is a genuine inner transformation towards a more loving, contented and whole person.

children.text: Can we love unconditionally?

Inside each human being resides their spirit, which is a source of pure love. This pure love does not discriminate, it just flows out to everything and everyone. If we all have that potential within us, what stops us from manifesting it? If we are truly honest with ourselves, we all have certain prejudices, insecurities or self interests which prevent us from being able to love everyone equally, including ourselves. These all stem from our attachments, which can be seen in the smallest moments of our life. For example, at a buffet do we reach to first fill our own plate, or the plate of another? Are we more attached to our own material needs, or are we thinking of someone else’s need?

Attachments are a very human nature, which occur within us all. However, the spirit brings us above this nature, to become a divine personality. The more we can detach from within, and come closer to our spirit, the more love will just spontaneously pour out from us in every direction.
An all-knowing, organising power

The impulse to care for ourselves before others often comes from a fear of what will happen otherwise. Who will care for me if I don’t? If I have a desire, how will it be fulfilled if I don’t make it happen?

When we are in a true state of meditation, and our final chakra, the Sahasrara, at the top of our head opens, we get connected to the all pervading energy of the universe which surrounds us. This energy makes everything happen. It organises, creates and destroys. When we are in connection with this energy it knows all of our needs and desires. It takes care of us, if we let it. In other words, if we are detached.

children.text: Every moment is an opportunity

Being connected to the all pervading power around you has the potential to fill your days with real magic and joy. Each small and mundane moment is an opportunity to see something miraculous take place before your eyes. Anytime you feel bored, or alone, or stressed, you can simply try raising your kundalini and asking for help - see what happens! The sheer surprise and delight of what ensues can make any normal day feel like the greatest discovery.
A source of security

When you start experiencing the immense power of this energy all around you, and how it organises and takes care of you, you gain a profound sense of peace and security. A feeling that you’re not alone, that you’re taken care of  - this is what gives you the ultimate comfort in life. When things just flow, you stop worrying and planning and trying to control. This saves so much time, energy and attention - you just feel so much less tired!
What will you ask for?

Start small, but then consider what it really is that you want in life. You can have fun experimenting with this relationship by asking for help with mundane everyday things such as needing traffic to move when you’re running late, or help with a job interview that you’re nervous about. However, the potential of this power is infinite, and it can work out your deepest desires for what you want to achieve in this lifetime. It can help you to transform and to become an ever-flowing source of love and peace for this world. What will you ask for?

children.text: Fire element

In Sahaja Yoga, we use the elements of nature to bring our subtle system into balance. As water is used to soothe the right channel, the fire element helps to invigorate the left channel. The light from the fire eliminates the negative energy within us and the warmth thaws the coldness that slows the left channel down.
Problems of the left side

There are many things in our day to day life that pull us away from being in a balanced state. As you’ve learned in earlier units, our mind is constantly drawing us away from the present, either into the future or back into the past. When our left channel is affected, we can feel lethargic, sad, unable to stop thinking about the past and often have a negative view on life. Rather than being a person’s ‘personality’, this is actually a left sided blockage that can be addressed by using techniques such as candle treatment to clear the left side.

Ongoing problems on the left side which do not improve immediately can be related to our past, our families and our ancestors. These can cause a weakness in our chakras and can take some persistent treatment to strengthen and clear out. Try not to blame yourself or others for these kinds of blockages, but remain patient and persist with the treatment, in time things should improve.
Level Up

If you frequently feel heaviness in the left side or feel that it takes a long time to clear out, you can try using a three candle treatment instead of just one. This involves sitting on the ground for meditation, placing one candle behind your left hip, one candle in front of your left knee with your left hand pointing towards it, and using the third candle to work on yourself like in this unit’s guided meditation.
When not to use candle treatment

Candle treatment must not be used when one’s right hand is hot. If this is the case and your left channel is still catching, opt to clear your left channel with the earth element so that the heat is not made worse by the fire. You can do this by either meditating directly on the ground outside, or by simply placing your right hand on/towards the ground while keeping your left hand open in your lap. You can also reduce the heat in your right side with a foot soak, as suggested in Unit 1.

children.text: The joy of innocence

Innocence is at the root of joy. Often known and experienced intuitively in childhood, when we are unbothered by ego and the accumulated conditionings brought by life, innocence is an innate childlike power that brings us joy and a natural excitement for life. Recall yourself as a child: how easily you laughed and found play in the everyday. Under normal circumstances.

To reassert innocence and rediscover natural joy we need one plain direction, live simply. Practical techniques include: regular meditation, connection with nature, cultivation of clean thoughts and desires, and self-loving introspection and correction. Through practical interventions like these we can successfully empower ourselves to rediscover our innate innocence and childlike joy once again. While keeping in mind, it was never lost in the first place, only covered.
When we are in union with ourselves and harmony with the world around joy naturally and spontaneously flows. Like that of a child.
Innocence is not ignorance

At times, people may equate innocence and ignorance together, giving rise to the unproductive view that innocence weakens us, rather than acting as a natural power that insulates and protects us from the corrosive hardships we may encounter in life. The belief directly links with the natural erosion of innocence many experience as they age and encounter more of the world. However, when a person attempts, in ignorance, to protect themselves from pain and deception by discarding innocence for the cold handshake of cynicism and false maturity, they lose the hopeful power innocence provides.

Though the process is undertaken in an attempt to preserve oneself against repeated hardship or discomfort, experienced at some point in childhood or youth, we rob ourselves if we sacrifice innocence and joyfulness to this process. Pessimism or the jaded cynicism of adulthood are no weapon against the rising and falling of daily life. Intuitive being, that is in harmony with one's inner being and the world around, is necessary; and where is that found first and foremost? In the natural unbounded living of childhood joy.

Hope and an attitude that tends towards the light is what preserves and maintains us against the difficulties we may encounter in life; as well, they are each aspects of the childlike joy we seek to maintain when we talk about preserving innocence in Sahaja Yoga meditation.

Innocence naturally grounds and sustains us. Therefore, cultivate an awareness that uplifts and sustains your joyfulness and directs your attention to the simple beauties of life, found all around you. Therefore, we may learn about the world and reduce our natural ignorance to the things we do not know, without lessening our grounding in the sustaining powers of the earth and the innocence inherent to each of us since childhood and birth.
Shri Ganesha an archetype of innocence

Often abstract qualities can be better understood through example, either by use of symbolism or archetypes. Archetypes can be understood as a pattern or model of human behaviour that repeats through history and across cultures. Universal human principles such as: love, discipline, self-mastery, mentorship, and leadership are all archetypes that exist and are expressed across human societies and culture, regardless of religion or race, geography or place of origin.

An archetypal example we can use is Shri Ganesha, the famously joyful, elephant-headed primordial son of Shri Shiva and Shri Parvati. His elephant head, discerning and wise, picks through the tricky maze of joylessness and false desire, maintaining steady and unobstructed righteous direction.

The remover of obstacles, with four hands facing the four cardinal directions (like a swastika) Shri Ganesha is the guide and propellent, pushing us toward the most generative and nourishing direction, aligned with our Spirit. The qualities of Shri Ganesha manifest inside each one of us as the wisdom, joy, and natural discretion present regularly since childhood.
His depiction symbolically represents many of these qualities:
Innocence and wisdom in the serene head of an elephant
Child-like joy and innocence in the body of a child
Remover of obstacles to spiritual growth by the weapons and tools held in his hands
Guidance from a cardinal centre, represented by four arms and symbolic spinning swastika
Om (ॐ) the primordial first sound associated with Ganesha and the start of spiritual journey from the mooladhara chakra

All the symbolic depictions of Shri Ganesha can be used to understand the archetype of innocence manifesting inside us. Shri Ganesha is a single example from a pantheon of archetypal expressions across human culture and history. Many can be used, but he represents the many subtle points that constitute the mooladhara chakra and the joy of innocence most directly.

children.text: The Aum

The Aum is the primordial sound of the universe, when it was first created. The three sounds, ‘A’ ‘U’ and ‘M’ resonate with the three energy channels within us. By reciting these sounds, both separately and together, we can cleanse our energy channels and nourish their powers within us.
Cleansing energy channels with AUM

When using sound to cleanse our subtle system we should keep our attention on the specific area we want to cleanse. E.g. When we cleanse our left channel our attention should be on the left side of our body. We can also use our hands to help direct the flow of vibrations. Below is an outline of how to cleanse the three energy channels using ‘AUM’.
Left Channel (channel of pure desire)
Sound: long A (mouth slightly open).
Position: Left hand open in your lap, right hand on the ground.
Right Channel (channel of pure action)
Sound: long U (round 'opera'-mouth).
Position: Right hand open in your lap, left arm bent at the elbow with palm face back and fingertips towards the sky..
Central Channel (channel of evolution)
Sound: long M (mouth open just so much that you get a tickling feeling in your lips).
Position: Both hands open in your lap.

You can repeat these sounds several times in the corresponding positions, or until you begin to feel cool in your open hand. You can then say the complete ‘AUM’ sound with your hands on your lap or with your right hand on the top of your head (the Sahasrara chakra).
Bija Mantras for every chakra

As you have learnt from this step’s meditation, each chakra has a certain sound which resonates when the Kundalini passes through. The number of times that sound is repeated corresponds to the number of petals (sub-plexuses) of that chakra. For your reference, here is a list of the Bija mantras for each chakra.

Note: Mantras should never be said mechanically, or in a rush. There is no need to say a mantra for every chakra in any given meditation. Use your discretion to feel which mantras should be said at which time, and do it with your full attention.

children.text: Universal Love: the Comfort of the Spirit
"God's meeting place with man is in the heart, and in a still small
voice he speaks; and he who hears is still.”
(The Aquarian Gospel of Christ, ch. 26)

The spirit and the experience of love and joy itself are one and the same. When we are in union with our spirit, our true self, we experience a universal sense of love and joy that is all-encompassing and greater than any single individual. This is the point where we experience connection with God, the universal being beyond ourselves that connects all people and things together. However, misidentifications that take us away from our true selves, prevent us from always experiencing this state.
“When all desires that cling to the heart are surrendered
(i.e. misidentifications), then a mortal becomes immortal, and
even in this world he is one with Brahman (i.e. absolute being).
When all the ties that bind the heart are unloosened,
then a mortal becomes immortal. This is the sacred teaching.
One hundred and one subtle ways come from the heart.
One of them rises to the crown of the head. This is the way
that leads to immortality; the others lead to different ends.
Always dwelling within all beings is the Atman, the
Purusha, the Self, a little flame in the heart. Let one with
steadiness withdraw him from the body even as an inner
stem is withdrawn from its sheath. Know this pure immortal
light; know in truth this pure immortal light.”
(The Upanishads, trans. Juan Mascaro, pg. 66)

The Upanishads reference the spirit and the barriers we create in the heart if we remain attached to false ideas or identifications preventing us from seeing our true selves. From the heart there are “one hundred and one subtle ways” but only one leads, by the kundalini energy, to the crown of the head: our Sahasrara. Into the space that transcends our small mind and conditionings.

When we discard false identifications about our Self (e.g. family, job, education, nationality) we become fully connected with the spirit. Then, through the raising of the kundalini, we become unified with the all pervading spirit, the Paramatman: Universal Divine Love. In this state we feel immense peace and bliss, and enter a deep state of tranquility and comfort. The love naturally stored within becomes transparent and the love naturally flowing around, enters and transforms us. Through this state we connect to the world and people around us and become unified with the all-pervading love of the Spirit.

children.text: What constricts our creativity?

The quality of creativity comes from our Swadisthan chakra, located in our lower abdomen area. When this chakra is weak or gets blocked, we can have difficulty finding inspiration to express our creativity. This often happens simply because we are thinking or planning too much. This heats up the right aspect of our Swadisthan and makes our attention scattered.

Creativity flows best when we are in the present, without thoughts. Artists often talk about a ‘flow state’ that they get into where they are not mentally conceiving their art, rather it is just flowing through them. For this to occur, some level of surrender is required. When we seek to control a process through our ego, we are limited by our own ideas and we cannot enter this ‘flow state’ and discover new forms of expression.
How to nourish the Swadisthana chakra
Here are some simple affirmations that we can say for the three aspects of our Swadisthan chakra:
Left Aspect:
‘Mother Kundalini, by your grace I am the pure knowledge that acts.’
Right Aspect:
‘I am not the doer. Mother Kundalini, you do everything, I do nothing.’
Central Aspect:
‘Mother Kundalini, please give me pure knowledge and creativity.’

Footsoak is a very powerful technique for cleansing the Swadisthan chakra as it uses both the earth and the water elements for drawing out excess heat. If we feel that our mind is racing and we can’t settle down to a creative task, a short foot soak can really help us to get into a more calm and surrendered state. To learn more about this go to Explore>>Techniques in this app.

If our attention is particularly poor, or we feel a lot of excess heat or agitation, we can also use an ice pack over our right Swadisthan during meditation to cool down our attention. You can learn more about this by going to Explore>>Techniques in this app.
How to recognise enlightened creativity?

There are numerous artistic works in the world, some resonate with us, some don’t. There are also different reasons for wanting to engage with art, sometimes just to make us feel good, other times to make us think about what the artist is trying to express. When we view creativity through the lens of a meditator, we can try asking ourselves ‘Was this created in a state of pure inspiration, without thought? Or did it come from the ego of the artist?’.

The reason that this question is pertinent is because depending on the answer the art will have a different impact on our own state. When art has come through an ego-driven process of thought and analysis, the result may cause us to think or feel a strong emotion, as the artist intended. However, when creativity comes through a process of pure inspiration, the result usually has a soothing effect on our subtle system, sometimes bringing us quickly into a state of thoughtlessness, like time standing still. We may even perceive a subtle cool breeze on our hands or on the top of our heads.

You can try experimenting with this phenomenon. Either when looking at art, listening to music, watching a dance or theatre performance, reading literature, or engaging with any other artform, just observe your state. You can even try holding out your hands to see if you can perceive any vibrations.
Here are some quotes from artists who claim that their art flowed through them from pure inspiration:
“I want to paint the way a bird sings.”- Claude Monet (Painter)
“The experience of art is spiritual, a reflection of the divine in the material world.” -Rabindranath Tagore (Poet)
‘The music of this opera [Madame Butterfly] was dictated to me by God; I was merely instrumental in putting it on paper and communicating it to the public.’ - Giacomo Puccini (Composer)

"Every block of stone has a statue inside it and it is the task of the sculptor to discover it." "I am only a tool in the hands of God, a mere instrument for his divine creations." - Michelangelo (Sculptor and Painter)
‘Straightaway the ideas flow in upon me, directly from God.’ - Johannes Brahms (Composer)

children.text: Guilt keeps us stuck in the past
If we are the Spirit, the pure unfiltered love and joy of our being: how can we be guilty?

In the state of love and joy we can see ourselves clearly, without ego or reaction from our limited conditionings and expectations. In the light of love and self-acceptance we clearly separate good from bad and take the necessary steps to overcome the past, allowing ourselves to grow.

Guilt is an escape we use to avoid facing ourselves, and where negative feelings and emotions are stored to evade responsibility and excuse introspection and change. The burden of guilt becomes enough to cushion against any wrongdoing, rather than actually facing the problem head-on and taking lessons that allow us to be transformed.

Rather than a solution, instead guilt works as a mechanism to trap ourselves in the past. Stuck attached to negative feelings and negative perceptions of ourselves, instead of learning and growing in the present.
How guilt negatively affects our meditation

When we allow guilt to direct our feelings the left vishuddhi becomes blocked, limiting the flow of vibrations along the left channel and preventing the joy from our spirit to rise to the sahasrara on the crown of our head.

As a result, left vishuddhi blockages seriously limit our wellbeing and contentment. Guilt manifests in very subtle ways we cannot always recognize immediately, but with vibrational sensitivity our awareness of these subtle changes increases.

To overcome guilt, focus your meditations on love, acceptance, and detachment from the past. As a child makes mistakes and falls down, be loving and kind and give yourself grace. “To err is human.” Be honest and diligent, but don’t allow yourself the subtle pleasure of guilty escapism. The attachment to guilt ties us to the past and prevents our presence and growth in the present.

children.text: Improving your Vishuddhi chakra through lifestyle

Vibrations are present all around you and in all things, they are an expression of the benevolent force of the all pervading, but it takes practice and depth to be able to work with them. The first step is to nourish your Vishuddhi chakra so that you can feel the cool or warm sensations on the various chakras within your hands.

There are passive and active ways to work on the Vishuddhi. Changes in your lifestyle and approach to situations will passively help to prevent damage to this Chakra. Reducing the use of sarcastic language, trying to always be honest with your words, in a gentle way without harshness, and not giving in to anger will soothe this chakra. Smoking (including vaping) will also damage your Vishuddhi chakra and make it more difficult for you to feel vibrations.
Nourishing your Vishuddhi chakra in meditation
There are also active steps you can take to bring this Chakra into balance. During your meditation you can give a bandhan to all three of the aspects of the Vishuddhi, left, right and centre.

left Vishuddhi

right Vishuddhi

central Vishuddhi

Try to ask questions, and see what answers you get. Generally speaking, over time collective consciousness has been rising and becoming more enlightened. It is certainly true that we do not live in a perfect world, but if one is able to take a step back and look at the whole of human history we can see that there has been a gradual refinement of the general population.

Consider how greatly the moral conscience of humanity has changed: things once accepted as normal are now for the most-part globally denounced. For most of history slavery was legal and widespread across nearly every civilisation, yet today it is condemned everywhere as a crime against human dignity. Torture and public execution, once carried out as justice and even as entertainment, are now regarded as barbaric. For almost the whole of history, the subordination of women was the unquestioned order. While there is still much progress to be made globally in women’s rights, the idea of their equality is now affirmed by most of the world - and where it is still denied, that denial is openly challenged rather than taken as natural.

When we look around it may sometimes be hard to see the progress, but in the consciousness of humanity as a whole, sublime qualities have been awakened. It is up to the individual to foster them within so that collectively we may continue to rise.
How to determine an incarnation?

There are many notable figures throughout history who have honorable characters and have worked hard to better society. There have also been many charlatans and false gurus who have claimed to be spiritual, or even messengers of God. What distinguishes a true divine personality?

An incarnation is not simply an enlightened soul. It is a being who took their birth with the soul purpose of raising humanity, through their every action, word and expression. At times their behaviours or decisions may have even been confusing or not overtly benevolent. This is because Divine logic often transcends human understanding, and in order to bring forth a new dimension of human awareness the preceding attitude/ideas had to be challenged.

Consider the example of Christ driving the merchants from the temple. Jesus was known as a teacher of love, peace and gentleness. Yet when he entered the great temple in Jerusalem, he found it crowded with merchants selling animals and money changers at their tables, turning a house of prayer into a place of trade. In anger he overturned their tables and drove them all out. To the people this seemed shocking and unlike the gentle man they knew, and it turned the temple's rulers against him. Yet behind his anger was a clear message: the house of God is meant for worship, not for profit, and what is sacred can never be bought or sold. What seemed like a sudden loss of his gentleness was, in truth, his boldest defence of devotion — a refusal to let the love of God be turned into a marketplace.

Using our vibratory awareness we can decipher who indeed was a true incarnation. By holding out our hands and asking a simple question, ‘Was ____ a divine incarnation?’ we can perceive the answer through the sensations we feel. A clear, cool breeze indicates an affirmative answer, while heat or tingling suggests a negative. You can try experimenting yourself by putting your attention on different prominent religious/cultural figures and see what answers you get!

Forming the mantra
Below is the structure of a full mantra:
OM, TWAMEVA SAKSHAT
SHRI (…) SAKSHAT
SHRI ADI-SHAKTI MATAJI,
SHRI NIRMALA DEVI,
NAMOH NAMAHA
Shri Adi Shakti

‘Adi’ is sanskrit translates to ‘primordial’, and ‘Shakti’ means ‘feminine power’. Adi Shakti is therefore the primordial feminine power that permeates all of creation, which is the source of creation itself. The Kundalini is the reflection of this power within all of us. We refer to Adi Shakti (using the prefix Shri to show reverence) as she is the integration of all forms of Divine energy. Therefore any deity or divine quality we are trying to invoke within ourselves is merely an aspect of Her.

While this primordial feminine power is known by the name of Adi Shakti in Hinduism and Sikhism, there are many references to it by different names in other religions and cultures. The Tao Te Ching describes the Tao as the mother of all things and as a "mysterious female," the gateway and root of heaven and earth. In Mesopatamia
Tiamat
is the primordial mother, the waters from whose very body the cosmos is formed.

In Judasim The Shekhinah is the indwelling divine presence — grammatically feminine, and understood in Kabbalah as the feminine aspect of God. In Gnosticism Sophia ("Wisdom") is the divine feminine emanation associated with the soul and the animating principle of the cosmos, and early traditions of Christianity spoke of the Holy Spirit in maternal terms.

In all of these traditions the feminine divine is understood to be the creative energy, while the masculine aspect of God the witness. Therefore all manifestations of this creative energy, in the form of the incarnations and their divine qualities reflected within us, are a part of Her.
The importance of attention

When we invoke these mantras, our attention is what gives them power. If we mindlessly read a list of mantras, not only will they be unlikely to have much of an affect on our chakras, but such a practice could also cause damage to our Vishuddhi chakra as we use our voice in a wrong way. We should be aware that we are inviting a Divine subtle energy to be manifested within us, and it should be done with the proper respect and sincerity. It is much better to say fewer mantras with full attention and heart than to recite many with shallow attention.

children.text: The shortfalls of moral philosophies

Moral philosophies, systems of morality created by language, logic or laws all tend to face the same problem at one time or another, that their logic inevitably leads to contradictions, and outcomes that are clearly intuitively immoral. There are examples of this across both western and eastern traditions.

In Kantian ethics, where moral rules must be universalisable and never self defeating, outcomes can be produced which contradict the moral aims. The classic example is the scenario where a murderer asks you where your friend is hiding, your duty to tell the truth conflicts with your duty to protect innocent life, and Kant famously argued that even then you must not lie.

The same problems exist within Confucian ethics. The duty of filial piety can conflict with the duty towards righteousness. Confucius argued that in the situation where a father had stolen a sheep, the morally upright son would cover for the father, because familial loyalty outweighs impartial justice. Applied rigidly to a whole society, this could lead to a culture of tribalism within families or clans and a lack of impartial rule of law, lowering overall social trust.
Lessons from Indian epics

The two Indian literary epics, the Mahabharata and the Ramayana both help us to understand the concept of dharma, as distinct from a written philosophy. Shri Rama obeys dharma and accepts exile in the forest, and in almost all respects sticks to the extremely strict moral codes of the time. However later, when Shabari, a low born woman, presents him with fruit, he breaks his rigid moral code out of acceptance of the love and affection she has shown. She pierced the skin of each fruit with her teeth, to check that they were all sweet, so that he would have good fruit to eat.

This act was against the codes of the time, as it rendered the food impure as it had touched someone else's mouth. Also accepting fruit from someone of a much lower social status was inappropriate for the time. This small act opens a crack in the otherwise extremely rigid moral code adhered to within the epic, and allows the reader to understand that there is more to Dharma than strict adherence to a code.

In the Mahabharata it is established that Shri Krishna was incarnated to protect true dharma, as it had become a dry and rigid system, binding its adherents to strict structures that produced absurd outcomes. At the beginning of the story, the oldest pandava Yudhishthira, accepts a challenge to a gambling match with the Kauravas that he knows is rigged. However, by the moral codes of the time, he could not refuse a challenge, and ended up losing everything the brothers own, their kingdom, and wife, Draupadi. The Kauravas then begin to disrobe Draupadi, and the only defence that any of her relatives or the elders of the court tried to mount was whether she was truly the Kauravas property or not.

This is one of the most clear examples of the failure of “proper conduct” to prevent injustice. Everyone in the court was bound by social and moral codes, respect for elders, obedience to the king, adherence to rules of wager and consequence, but those very structures created a situation where a grave moral violation was unfolding in front of them.

The episode showed how the strict or formal adherence to what they understood as dharma had become paralyzing when the system itself was being used unjustly. This episode was the cause of the entire Mahabharata war, and the rest of the epic is replete with examples of Shri Krishna breaking the codes of the time to ensure a truly moral outcome.
Using our inner guide

Moral philosophies matter because they help people think through the consequences of their actions and recognise the broader social responsibilities that come with how they choose to live. However they will always produce contradictions, and cannot be a good all round individual guide to the best way for each of us personally to act. Dharma (in a similar way to Taoism/Daoism) is a recognition of this problem that allows us to go a step further. By recognising that the things we do, our thoughts, and feelings have an impact on our chakras, we can intuitively feel what is best for us, and what is damaging. Our subtle mechanisms can be a much stronger, attuned and living guide for our lives than a system of logic, and they will allow us to grow and flourish in a way which does not bind us to excessive rigidity or contradiction.

children.text: Searching for security

The most common response to fear is to seek protection externally, many try to find it in wealth, status, relationships, knowledge, or power. It feels natural and reasonable to respond to fear in this way. The fear within can abate for a time when you have the mental reassurance that you have a shield to respond to threats. In the modern world, these threats are not usually physical in nature. They are often social: fear of criticism, rejection, embarrassment, or failure. They can also be interpersonal, fear of losing someone, or economic, fear of losing one's livelihood or home.

However, it is easy to recognise that the strategies that we use to respond to fear are only temporary measures. Money, status, relationships etc… can all be lost, and even if they are present, the knowledge that they could be lost still creates fear. This fear creates a spiritual prison, where we are never truly free, and our actions and thoughts are coloured by, or filtered through a lens of fear, of potential loss and of failure.

Fear often creates the very suffering it seeks to avoid. A fearful person may avoid challenges and remain stuck, allowing opportunities for joy and liberation to fall by the wayside. They may hesitate to speak truthfully, damaging relationships or themselves. In trying to protect themselves from pain, they end up restricting their own freedom.
How we can deal with fear

The spiritual response to fear is not to try to force your mind into the delusion that negative things will not happen to you. The mind creates scenarios, imagines losses, and anticipates suffering, it is a tool for risk mitigation and planning, attempting to help you make what are mentally sensible and realistic decisions. Rising above also does not mean becoming reckless or exhibiting blind courage. To move beyond fear is to have a complete integration of your mind, heart and spirit. To live completely in the present and in Reality. Fear is often a warning sign, information that can let you know your attention has shifted away from reality, and from the awareness of the spirit

As you grow, the Kundalini nourishes the Centre Heart, which brings a sense of innate security, unattached to external circumstances, which allows you to stay present, connected and detached. The mind is also soothed by your established meditative state, and doesn't run away with projections and doubts, allowing you to act clearly with balance and dignity. The more these qualities awaken, the more fear is naturally replaced by a quiet and stable fearlessness.

children.text: Meditation is the road to Growth

The Kundalini nourishes your being when you meditate. When you are in thoughtless awareness (i.e. in meditation) your attachments and reactions are calm for that time. You can see things more clearly without your inner reactions clouding your understanding. After being in this state it is much easier to respond to situations in a genuine way, without your ego or your expectations weighing on you. Generally the situations you find yourself in resolve much better as a result. Meditation is a journey with a more enlightened self as the goal.
Meditative Growth transforms from within

We often look outwards for spiritual and personal growth. From books to courses, to inspiring people, to seminars, people seek to better themselves with influences from others. Through regular meditation you develop an innate understanding and intuition of how to grow and which situations and responses will be good for you, and which won't.
Growth is Spontaneous

Through introspection based on your meditation experience you may realise that there are aspects of your personality you would like to work on. This idea could be daunting, and you may feel that you need to wrestle with your mind or emotions to overcome certain barriers. However, growth through meditation happens very naturally, and in a way that is often unexpected. Just like a plant grows quietly through nourishment, consistent meditation allows your being to be nourished by the Kundalini. The barriers within you can then unexpectedly break down, almost without you realising, and you become a more evolved personality.
Growth is Nourishing

What does personal growth look like? A person who has been able to grow is a nourishing presence to those around them. They have the ability to be compassionate and loving, without taking on a burden from others. They have energy to pursue the things they find important and to enjoy life, because they aren't as burdened with their reactions or scars from the past. They are able to follow their intuition, make decisions which are beneficial to their spirit, and they are able to recuperate from stressful or high intensity scenarios effectively. They have cultivated an inner calm and certainty, with their awareness guided by their Kundalini and the all pervading power, and create a feeling of calm and clarity in others around them. Collective Growth helps everyone.

The more people who undertake this journey of self growth, the more the collective humanity benefits. As individuals become more compassionate, more understanding, have more energy, and are guided more and more by this inner connection with the all pervading power, they are able to effect positive outcomes on the situations that come their way. Each one of these small interactions and moments can add up to a lot of good for the whole.
